title: Designing and Simulating Forecasting Questions with EDSL
summary: How to use LLM-powered agents to generate structured datasets from ranges, rationales, and free-text forecasts
body_text: Designing and Simulating Forecasting Questions with EDSL How to use LLM-powered agents to generate structured datasets from ranges, rationales, and free-text forecasts Expected Parrot and Robin Horton Sep 23, 2025 Whether they’re answered by AI agents or human participants, forecasting questions often require more structure than other types of survey questions. For example, when asking about inflation or interest rates, you might want a range forecast (e.g., “between 2% and 4%”) rather than just a single number. You may also want to capture the reasoning behind a forecast, allowing respondents to answer in their own words while still recording the details in a format that can be analyzed consistently. With EDSL , you can design forecasting questions in whatever form makes sense — from open-ended free text to tightly specified schemas — and have the responses automatically returned as a well-structured dataset. This makes it easy to experiment with different ways of framing questions for both AI agents and humans while ensuring that outputs remain standardized, comparable, and ready for analysis. In this post, we’ll walk through a simple example using EDSL to design a forecasting question, administer it in multiple formats to an agent persona powered by an LLM, and inspect the results. We’ll also show how unstructured free-text answers can be transformed into structured data automatically. For more details on the methods used, see our documentation page. EDSL is an open-source package for simulating surveys with AI agents and LLMs of your choice. It is maintained by Expected Parrot and available under the MIT License. Please join our Discord to ask questions, submit feature requests, and connect with other researchers! 1. Defining Forecasting Questions Let’s start with a forecasting question about U.S. CPI inflation in December 2025. We’ll frame it two ways, using different EDSL question types that allow us to specify the format of the model’s response: Structured (dictionary format): where we prompt a model to provide a lower bound, an upper bound, and rationale. Free text: where a model can respond however it chooses. We combine the questions in a survey to administer them together. Note that by default questions are administered async, so we can get choose whether to generate independent answers or (optionally) add within-survey memory (here we do not): from edsl import QuestionDict, QuestionFreeText, Survey question_text = """What will the year-over-year U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation rate be in December 2025? Provide your forecast as a range (e.g., 2.0%-4.0%). The range should reflect the interval you believe has a 90% chance of containing the true outcome, based on BLS published data.""" q1 = QuestionDict( question_name = "q1", question_text = question_text, answer_keys = ["range_lower_bound", "range_upper_bound", "rationale"], value_types = [float, float, str], value_descriptions = [ "The lower bound value of your forecasted range.", "The upper bound value of your forecasted range.", "The rationale for your forecast." ] ) q2 = QuestionFreeText( question_name = "q2", question_text = question_text ) survey = Survey(questions = [q1, q2]) 2. Creating an Agent and Running the Survey We’ll give our agent a (very) simple persona — a “professional forecaster” — and then select a model to generate the answers. EDSL works with models from many popular service providers; you can check available models, token prices and performance here . To administer the survey we simply add the agent and model, and then run the job: from edsl import Agent, Model agent = Agent(traits = {"persona":"professional forecaster"}) model = Model("gemini-2.5-flash", service_name = "google") results = survey.by(agent).by(model).run() 3. Inspecting Results The results are a formatted dataset that includes columns of information about the questions, agent, model, tokens, raw responses and other details of the job. We can inspect them at Expected Parrot or in a notebook. Here we print just the answers in a table: We can flatten a dictionary answer for easier analysis (see methods for working with results SQL, pandas, or other tools): 3. Turning unstructured text into structured data We can also use other EDSL question types to reformat the free text response. Here we create a " scenario " for the text in order to add it to questions prompting a model to extract the range values (as floats) and summarize the rationale in the original answer: from edsl import Scenario, QuestionNumerical, QuestionFreeText, Survey # use the q2 answer as a Scenario in new questions unstructured_answer = results.select("q2").to_list()[0] s = Scenario({"unstructured_answer":unstructured_answer}) q1 = QuestionNumerical( question_name = "lower", question_text = "Identify the LOWER bound value in the following response: {{ scenario.unstructured_answer }}" ) q2 = QuestionNumerical( question_name = "upper", question_text = "Identify the UPPER bound value in the following response: {{ scenario.unstructured_answer }}" ) q3 = QuestionFreeText( question_name = "rationale", question_text = "Summarize the rationale provided in the following response: {{ scenario.unstructured_answer }}" ) survey = Survey(questions = [q1, q2, q3]) results = survey.by(s).by(model).run() # no agent used 4. Why This Matters Forecasting often benefits from a mix of formats: Structured formats make it easy to aggregate, compare, and analyze forecasts. Free text formats capture richer reasoning and context. By combining both in the same survey, you can explore how LLMs and human respondents differ in not just what they forecast, but how they explain their forecasts. Try It Yourself You can reproduce this workflow by installing EDSL: !uv pip install edsl -q Log in to Expected Parrot (your account comes with free credits for API calls to LLMs for getting started): from edsl import login login() Download the complete notebook for the code examples above here . Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support our work. A guest post by Robin Horton Co-Founder @ Expected Parrot Subscribe to Robin

title: The role of GIS field data in mining for subsidence risk mitigation
summary: Explore how GIS field data in mining enhances safety and productivity by providing real-time observations for effective risk management.
body_text: Land subsidence threatens safety, compliance, and productivity across mining operations. Reliable GIS field data in mining ensures that every observation, from surface cracks to elevation shifts, flows into models that guide risk detection and response. Structured field measurements provide the foundation, while remote sensing, satellite imagery, and digital elevation models (DEMs) add the broader context needed to keep subsidence models accurate. Digital platforms tie these inputs together in real time, turning raw field observations into actionable strategies for safer, more resilient operations. Key insights GIS field data in mining must be accurate, frequent, and structured to keep subsidence models reliable and actionable. Digital field collection eliminates delays caused by handwritten notes, spreadsheets, or email-based reporting (legacy methods that slow decision-making). Configurable platforms allow mining operations teams to adapt quickly as blasting patterns or monitoring requirements change. Standardized workflows make mining field data usable across engineers, compliance leads, and planners. Proactive subsidence management requires linking real-time field data directly to GIS-based planning model s. Combining field data with remote sensing, satellite imagery, and DEMs improves subsidence detection across critical mine structures like benches and haul roads. Mining teams face constant pressure to track land subsidence before it disrupts operations. Even small shifts in stability can damage infrastructure, stall production, and invite regulatory attention. Field crews collect huge volumes of information every day, but without structured field mapping workflows and consistent GIS data, much of it never reaches the systems used for planning. Integrated GIS workflows connect field reporting with decision-making to keep subsidence risk under control. How weak field data undermines GIS subsidence models Mining operations rely on stable ground, predictable patterns, and accurate data to manage every phase of development. Land subsidence disrupts all three by weakening infrastructure , delaying schedules, and increasing regulatory risk. Early indicators of subsidence like cracking, slope movement, or elevation change require consistent observation and fast action. Without real-world field data, teams risk missing those warnings before they become serious problems. Geospatial models help identify where subsidence may occur, but the quality of those GIS data insights depends on what feeds them. If the inputs don’t reflect current, site-specific conditions, your team is reacting to old information. Using outdated inputs exposes operations to cascading risks across scheduling, safety, cost control, and environmental impact. This includes mis‑calibrated geostatistical functionality when models lack recent geological data and spatial data inputs. Every missed measurement becomes another blind spot in an already shifting environment. GIS field data in mining must be accurate, frequent, and consistent. Occasional inspections or disconnected reports fail to capture how fast conditions can change. Rainfall, dewatering, blasting, and excavation all accelerate movement below the surface. Waiting days to log those shifts delays the model, and weakens its value as a planning tool. Mining teams need better ways to collect and apply the GIS data they already generate daily. Those improvements start with structured field mapping workflows. The role of GIS field data in mining risk detection GIS platforms are critical for detecting subsidence risk across large, complex mining sites. When working with accurate inputs, they offer visibility across benches, haul roads, drainage zones, and infrastructure corridors. They help geotechnical engineers, compliance leads, and environmental consultants model risk clearly, document response plans, and adapt to new conditions without delay. But without high-quality mining field data, that system stops working. GIS models gain precision when field observations are combined with satellite imagery and remote sensing data. Digital elevation models highlight slope changes, while geological layers show how nearby conditions might impact stability. When these elements feed into a unified GIS view, teams spot deformation sooner and act with full spatial context. Digital field data collection solves that problem. Teams record elevation benchmarks, tension cracks, surface deformation, and terrain anomalies directly in the field. For positional accuracy, many crews pair their data collection apps with GNSS receivers, often with dual-frequency setups , to reduce atmospheric error and maintain centimeter-level precision even in challenging terrain. Every entry is timestamped, location-tagged, and formatted for immediate use. Teams avoid delays between collection and application because the platform validates and formats records automatically. And analysts receive clean, structured inputs that are ready for modeling and mapping without manual steps. That connection between field conditions and GIS insight turns surface observations into actual mitigation strategies. When every team works from the same, real-time inputs, the models help identify high-risk zones before they escalate. Standardized field mapping workflows make the difference between consistent monitoring and fragmented reporting. When GIS field data in mining operations feeds directly into planning models, every observation contributes to proactive risk management. Enrich models with remote sensing, DEMs, and geology Satellite imagery, remote sensing, and field-collected measurements each reveal part of the picture. When overlaid with DEMs, geological maps, and geophysical data, those layers help geological engineers identify patterns of deformation early. That spatial context speeds triage around benches, haul roads, and drainage zones before small shifts escalate into costly failures. Field collection methods must keep pace with mining operations Mining field data loses value when collection lags behind site activity. Traditional processes like handwritten notes, emailed photos, or spreadsheet uploads create unnecessary drag. Valuable insights get buried in inboxes, misfiled across systems, or delayed until the next scheduled update. Every layer of friction reduces your ability to act early and accurately. Digital tools and GIS mapping equipment eliminate those gaps. Crews log measurements as they work, without returning to trailers or workstations. Forms reflect inspection protocols, and data flows straight into GIS and reporting tools without re-entry or reformatting. Teams move quickly because the system doesn’t force them to slow down for documentation, while streamlined GIS workflows ensure that critical observations directly feed predictive models. Digital field tools that capture GIS field data in mining must support offline functionality across every part of the collection process. Crews work in remote or low-signal areas, and field mapping workflows can’t pause for coverage. A well-designed platform records structured GIS data offline, then syncs automatically when connected without reformatting, reentry, or manual processing. Teams capture observations during active work, not after the fact or from memory. Configurable systems give mining teams more control As mining operations move through new phases, reporting requirements change, often faster than static systems can accommodate. When blasting sequences shift or monitoring expands into new areas, for example, field collection tools must adjust immediately. Otherwise, teams end up tracking outdated parameters that no longer reflect current site priorities. Mining teams need to adjust reporting as conditions shift, without losing time or introducing inconsistency. A digital field data collection platform designed for configurability allows supervisors to revise forms and update logic directly. As inspection requirements evolve, the platform adapts immediately, keeping field reporting aligned with current site activity. Customizable field mapping workflows help to make sure that new requirements are captured without slowing work down or creating version conflicts. Standardization doesn’t have to mean rigidity. You control what gets tracked, how it’s structured, and where it integrates. TThe system stays consistent across teams, while remaining able to adapt quickly when needed. Built-in project management ties assignments, SLAs, and status updates directly to field reporting, keeping inspection cycles aligned with blast schedules and monitoring zones. Structured mining field data supports compliance and planning Land subsidence in mining carries safety, environmental , and permitting consequences that demand clear documentation. Regulators want proof of what was observed, when it was logged, and who verified the entry. If surface movement causes downstream damage, agencies look for evidence that monitoring was consistent and responses were timely. Field platforms that capture user, time, location, and conditions create auditable logs by default. Reports export in standard formats, inspection logs organized by date and region, and records reflect the actual work performed on-site. Structured field mapping workflows extend that reliability across the organization, giving engineers, planners, and compliance leads a shared source of GIS data. Teams use that data for analysis, environmental management reporting, and to demonstrate compliance with initiatives like worker safety policies or abandoned mine land program requirements. Staying ahead of subsidence Land subsidence is a serious challenge for mining operations, affecting safety, environmental stability, and long-term site management. GIS-based models help predict these risks, but their accuracy depends on real-world field data. Without consistent ground measurements and structured field reporting, mining teams may miss key warning signs, leading to unexpected damage, compliance issues, or operational delays. Digital field data collection keeps monitoring current, feeding predictive models with accurate information so decisions come sooner and risks are reduced. Subsidence will always be part of mining, but it doesn’t have to dictate operations. When field data is captured through structured field mapping workflows and carried into planning with integrated GIS workflows , risks are identified earlier and managed with full-picture clarity. The result is safer crews, stronger compliance, and uninterrupted productivity even under shifting ground conditions. Across the mining lifecycle from exploration to production, structured data linking field, lab, and map layers supports everything from targeting mineral deposits to controlling subsidence risk. And with clean, connected data, subsidence stops being a surprise and starts being something you’re ready for. title: Champions Oncology Reports Quarterly Revenue of $14.0 Million
summary: Champions Oncology, Inc. (Nasdaq:CSBR), a leading translational oncology research organization, today announced its financial results for its first quarter of fiscal 2026, ended July 31, 2025.
body_text: Positive start to FY 2026 with steady revenue, data growth and new leadership HACKENSACK, NJ / ACCESS Newswire / September 15, 2025 / Champions Oncology, Inc. (Nasdaq:CSBR), a leading translational oncology research organization, today announced its financial results for its first quarter of fiscal 2026, ended July 31, 2025. First Quarter and Recent Highlights: Total revenue of $14 million Adjusted EBITDA of $60,000 Appointment of Rob Brainin as Chief Executive Officer to lead the next phase of growth Rob Brainin, newly appointed CEO of Champions, commented, "It is great to be joining Champions at such an exciting inflection point. Our core services business - the backbone of our company - is strengthening and well positioned for sustained growth. At the same time, we are scaling our emerging data platform, which has already shown encouraging traction with leading biopharma partners. These complementary growth engines give us the opportunity to deepen our scientific impact, deliver innovative solutions to patients and customers, and create durable long-term value for shareholders. In parallel, our Corellia team continues to generate data demonstrating the potential of the compounds in our pipeline. Over the coming quarters, I look forward to working closely with our talented team to sharpen our strategy, invest in key capabilities, and build on Champions' culture of collaboration and scientific excellence." David Miller, CFO of Champions, added, "We opened the fiscal year with $14 million in revenue and adjusted EBITDA of $60,000. While revenue was slightly lower than the first quarter of last year, we achieved solid sequential growth that met our expectations and provides a strong foundation for the year. As we move forward, we anticipate continued topline expansion and margin improvement driven by a healthy services pipeline and growing demand for our proprietary data offerings. Our financial discipline and focus on profitable growth give us the flexibility to invest in strategic initiatives that will position Champions for long-term success." First Fiscal Quarter Financial Results Total oncology revenue for the first quarter of fiscal 2026 was $14.0 million compared to $14.1 million for the same period last year, consisting of a $400,000, or 3% decline in service revenue and a $300,000 increase in data license revenue. Total costs and operating expenses for the first quarter of fiscal 2026 were $14.5 million compared to $12.7 million for the first quarter of fiscal 2025, an increase of $1.8 million or 14.1%. For the first quarter of fiscal 2026, Champions reported a loss from operations of $527,000, including $208,000 in stock-based compensation, $358,000 in depreciation and amortization expenses, and a $20,000 charge for the disposal of lab equipment, compared to income from operations of $1.3 million, inclusive of $258,000 in stock-based compensation and $448,500 in depreciation and amortization expenses, in the first quarter of fiscal 2025. Adjusted EBITDA, which is defined as income from operations excluding stock-based compensation, depreciation and amortization expenses, and equipment disposal charges, was $59,000 for the first quarter of fiscal 2026 compared to adjusted EBITDA of $2.0 million in the first quarter of fiscal 2025. Cost of oncology revenue was $8.0 million, up $923,000, or 13.1%, from $7.1 million in the same period last year. The increase primarily reflects higher outsourced lab services for radiolabeling work, which will vary from quarter to quarter. Importantly, as we migrate this work into our own labs in the coming quarters, we anticipate a reduction in cost of sales and improvement in gross margins. Gross margin for the quarter was 43% compared to 50% in the prior year. Research and development expense for the three-months ended July 31, 2025 was $2.1 million, an increase of $628,000 or 43.2%, compared to $1.5 million for the three-months ended July 31, 2024. The increase reflected greater investment in sequencing and related costs to develop our data licensing platform. Sales and marketing expense for the three-months ended July 31, 2025 was $1.9 million, an increase of $176,000, or 10.5%, compared to $1.7 million for the three-months ended July 31, 2024. The increase was related to compensation expense to support the growth of our data license business. General and administrative expense for the three-months ended July 31, 2025 was $2.6 million, an increase of $43,000, or 1.7%, compared to $2.5 million for the three-months ended July 31, 2024 driven primarily from an increase in IT related costs. Net cash provided by operating activities was approximately $600,000 for the quarter, supported by receivables conversion and normal working capital activity, partially offset by a quarterly net loss. Net cash used in investing activities for the three-months ended July 31, 2025 was approximately $46,000 for lab and computer equipment. Net cash used in financing activities for the three-months ended July 31, 2025 was $14,000 resulting from financing lease payments slightly offset by proceeds from options exercises. The Company ended the quarter with cash on hand of approximately 10.3 million and no debt, providing us with a strong balance sheet and financial flexibility. title: États-Unis : TotalEnergies prend la Décision Finale d’Investissement avec ses partenaires pour le Train 4 de Rio Grande LNG, avec une participation directe de 10 % et un contrat d’enlèvement de 1,5 Mt de GNL
summary: Paris, le 10 septembre 2025 – TotalEnergies a signé des accords avec NextDecade pour prendre une participation de 10 % dans la coentreprise développant le Train 4 du projet Rio Grande LNG (RGLNG), une usine de gaz naturel liquéfié (GNL) située dans le sud du Texas. En plus des 10 % détenus directement, TotalEnergies détiendra indirectement près de […]
body_text: Paris, le 10 septembre 2025 – TotalEnergies a signé des accords avec NextDecade pour prendre une participation de 10 % dans la coentreprise développant le Train 4 du projet Rio Grande LNG (RGLNG), une usine de gaz naturel liquéfié (GNL) située dans le sud du Texas. En plus des 10 % détenus directement, TotalEnergies détiendra indirectement près de 7 % dans ce Train 4 en tant qu’actionnaire à hauteur de 17,1 % de NextDecade. Parallèlement, TotalEnergies, NextDecade (40 %) et leurs partenaires Global Infrastructure Partners (GIP, 36,9 %), GIC (7,9 %) et Mubadala (5,2 %) ont pris la Décision Finale d’Investissement (FID) pour le développement du Train 4. Ce quatrième train, d’une capacité d’environ 6 millions de tonnes par an (Mtpa), portera la capacité totale de l’usine à environ 24 Mtpa lorsqu’il sera mis en service en 2030. Le coût global du projet sera financé à environ 40 % par des fonds propres et 60 % par de la dette. « Nous nous réjouissons de la décision finale d’investissement du Train 4 de RGLNG. Ce projet, dont nous prélèverons 1,5 Mtpa, renforce notre capacité d’exportation de GNL depuis les États-Unis », a déclaré Stéphane Michel, Président de Gas, Renewables & Power chez TotalEnergies . « Il permet à TotalEnergies d’accéder à un GNL compétitif grâce à ses faibles coûts de production. Le GNL issu de ce quatrième train portera notre capacité d’exportation de GNL aux États-Unis à plus de 16 Mtpa d’ici 2030, consolidant ainsi notre part de marché mondiale de 10 % . » « Nous sommes ravis que TotalEnergies, notre plus grand client GNL et partenaire en capital pour la phase 1 de Rio Grande LNG, renforce son engagement envers notre projet à travers le Train 4 », a déclaré Matt Schatzman, Président-directeur général de NextDecade . « Le GNL exporté par TotalEnergies depuis notre projet fournira une énergie abordable, fiable et sécurisée aux clients du monde entier. » TotalEnergies avait déjà signé un contrat de vente et d’achat (SPA) avec NextDecade pour prélever 1,5 Mtpa pendant 20 ans de gaz naturel liquéfié issu du futur Train 4. TotalEnergies détient actuellement 16,7 % de la Phase 1 de Rio Grande LNG, qui comprend trois trains de liquéfaction en construction dans le sud du Texas, dont la mise en service est prévue en 2027, et à partir desquels TotalEnergies prélèvera 5,4 Mtpa. TotalEnergies détient également 17,1 % de NextDecade , actionnaire et opérateur de Rio Grande LNG. ***

title: Lloyd D. Smith
body_text: The founding organizing director for City First Bank, Lloyd D. Smith’s pioneering leadership in housing, community and economic development in the Washington Metropolitan area yields a long and storied list of accomplishments. As the President and CEO of the Marshall Heights Community Development Organization, during the 1980s and 1990s, Smith ushered in an era of unprecedented growth, leading the organization from an annual budget of $115,000 to over $5 million. Smith became well known for his signature single and multifamily housing and mixed-use retail properties, and for employing social service programs in the communities he helped develop. Prior to joining City First Bank, he had acquired some 27 years of federal and district government service and was a mayoral appointee to the Board of the National Capital Revitalization Corporation. He became Chairman and served as acting President of both organizations, and was featured in several documentaries. In 1991, Mr. Smith helped organize the visit of former First Lady Barbara Bush and Queen Elizabeth II of the United Kingdom to DC’s Ward 7; following her visit a street in the ward was named Queen Elizabeth’s Way. President Clinton toured the area in 1993. That same year, Lloyd Smith met with two-dozen community development leaders gathered in a Washington, DC church basement. Organizers were concerned about the toll on low-income neighborhoods from decades of divestment and discrimination. Confident that the marketplace could do a better job, they worked to create a financial institution to help neighborhoods that had been ignored. City First Bank launched in late 1998. Smith was the recipient of numerous national and international awards and honors, including the 1993 Local Minority Business Advocate Award; 1994 Points of Light Foundation Community Leadership Award; the DC Building Industry Association’s Community Service Award; and the Local Minority Business Advocate Award presented at the 8th Annual Salute to Blacks in Business. Following these illustrious accomplishments, Mr. Smith was inducted into the District of Columbia Hall of Fame Society in 2002.

title: Auth.js is now part of Better Auth
summary: Auth.js, formerly known as NextAuth.js, is now being maintained and overseen by Better Auth team
body_text: We’re excited to announce that Auth.js , formerly known as NextAuth.js, is now being maintained and overseen by Better Auth team. If you haven't heard of Auth.js, it has long been one of the most widely used open source authentication libraries in the JavaScript ecosystem. Chances are, if you’ve used ChatGPT , Google Labs , Cal.com or a million other websites, you’ve already interacted with Auth.js. Back Story about Better Auth and Auth.js Before Better Auth, Auth.js gave developers like us the ability to own our auth without spending months wrestling with OAuth integrations or session management. But as applications became more complex and authentication needs evolved, some of its limitations became harder to ignore. We found ourselves rebuilding the same primitives over and over. The Auth.js team recognized these challenges and had big ideas for the future, but for various reasons couldn’t execute them as fully as they hoped. That shared frustration and the vision of empowering everyone to truly own their auth started the creation of Better Auth. Since our goals aligned with the Auth.js team, we were excited to help maintain Auth.js and make auth better across the web. As we talked more, we realized that Better Auth was the best home for Auth.js. What does this mean for existing users? We recognize how important this project is for countless applications, companies, and developers. If you’re using Auth.js/NextAuth.js today, you can continue doing so without disruption—we’ll keep addressing security patches and urgent issues as they come up. But we strongly recommend new projects to start with Better Auth unless there are some very specific feature gaps (most notably stateless session management without a database). Our roadmap includes bringing those capabilities into Better Auth, so the ecosystem can converge rather than fragment. For teams considering migration, we’ve prepared a guide and we’ll be adding more guides and documentation soon. Final Thoughts We are deeply grateful to the Auth.js community who have carried the project to this point. In particular, the core maintainers- Balázs , who served as lead maintainer, Thang Vu , Nico Domino , Lluis Agusti and Falco Winkler -pushed through difficult phases, brought in new primitives, and kept the project alive long enough for this transition to even be possible. Better Auth beginning was inspired by Auth.js, and now, together, the two projects can carry the ecosystem further. The end goal remains unchanged: you should own your auth! For the Auth.js team's announcement, see GitHub discussion . title: Singapore Airliness KrisFlyer Devaluation Coming on November 1, 2025
summary: Singapore airlines just announced a devaluation of the Krisflyer Program
body_text: Singapore Airliness KrisFlyer Devaluation Coming on November 1, 2025 By Tim Qin - Updated: June 25, 2026 Singapore airlines just announced a devaluation of the Krisflyer Program Singapore Airlines is changing the KrisFlyer program on November 1, 2025. Saver and Advantage awards are going up, long-haul premium flights will take the biggest hit, and a new “Access Award” tier will bring dynamic pricing. Here’s what you need to know — and where the sweet spots still remain. What’s Changing on November 1 Singapore Airlines has confirmed a KrisFlyer devaluation effective November 1, 2025. Saver awards — the most popular way to redeem miles — will increase by about 5% on average. Advantage awards, which offer more availability at higher rates, will rise by 10–15%. The biggest impact is on Zone 10 routes (U.S. to Singapore), where business- and first-class Saver awards will jump 10–20%. Live SkyView Up-to-date results with Live Search. Search up to 25 airline loyalty programs up to 365 days in any fare class within 10-15 seconds See deals instantly with SkyView. SkyView constantly checks flights for the top 6,500 routes so you can see your results instantly. Try Live Search Join Now Try SkyView Join Now Live SkyView The New “Access Awards” Alongside higher chart pricing, Singapore Airlines is debuting Access Awards. These are dynamically priced awards that scale with demand, similar to how cash tickets are sold. On the plus side, Access Awards mean there will be more availability, especially on high-demand routes. The downside is that pricing will often be far higher — think 200,000 miles or more for a single Business Class seat during peak travel periods. Where It Hurts Most For premium travelers, the devaluation is felt most on Singapore Airlines’ flagship long-haul services: Nonstops to Singapore from major global gateways now run 112,500–117,000 miles in Business Class Saver and 154,000–156,000 miles in Suites Saver. Advantage rates, which already carried a premium, are now 15% higher, pushing Suites close to 280,000 miles one-way. These increases make aspirational redemptions like the world’s longest flight — Singapore to New York — significantly harder to book with miles. -Singapore Airlines Received World's first Boeing 787-10 Dreamliner The Sweet Spots That Survive Even with the increases, KrisFlyer retains some gems: Fifth freedom flights such as New York–Frankfurt or Houston–Manchester stay untouched at 81,000 miles in Business Class, still one of the best ways to experience Singapore Airlines without flying all the way to Asia. Intra-Asia routes like Singapore–Tokyo or Singapore–Seoul r emain solid at around 55,000 miles in Business Class — excellent value for six- to seven-hour flights. Short-haul economy redemptions, including Singapore–Bangkok, will actually drop slightly in cost, moving from 15,000 to 13,000 miles. Australia and New Zealand routes rise only about 5%, keeping them competitive for medium-haul premium travel. – Inside Singapore Airlines A380 Business Class Compartment. Final Thoughts KrisFlyer’s upcoming devaluation highlights a familiar trend: more miles for the same seat, especially in the cabins most travelers want. For those planning aspirational trips, there’s still time — tickets can be booked up to 355 days out, meaning travel deep into 2026 can still be locked in at today’s rates. While First Class and Suites awards on long-haul nonstops will become significantly more expensive, sweet spots like fifth freedom routes and intra-Asia flights ensure KrisFlyer still holds unique value. The key now is planning ahead — and making those bookings before November 1.

title: Functional Beverages Are Having a Moment

body_text: Walk into any grocery store or scroll TikTok, and you’ll see it: functional beverages are booming. Consumers are no longer just reaching for hydration or caffeine. They want drinks that deliver energy, protein, probiotics, or electrolytes while still being fun, flavorful , and social-media ready. According to Spate, the Energy, Sports, and Functional Drinks category is up +34.5% YoY in popularity — and the momentum shows no signs of slowing. Energy Drinks: Beyond the Buzz Energy drinks are still king, with a +148.5M avg monthly popularity YoY across Google Search and TikTok. But this isn’t just about a caffeine jolt anymore. TikTok hashtags like #preworkout, #gymtok, and #caffeine are fueling steady growth, while new players such as Alani Nu and Salud are taking share with playful branding and influencer-driven campaigns. The category is predicted to grow another +35.0% YoY, driven by next-gen innovation. Expect to see energy drinks infused with adaptogens, nootropics, and wellness ingredients that promise more than just alertness. Protein Coffee: The New Morning Ritual If energy drinks dominate the gym crowd, protein coffee is winning over the morning multitasker. With 85.1% of its popularity tied to TikTok, this trend is everywhere from gym bags to office desks. Hashtags like #highprotein, #icedcoffee, and #proteinshake show how consumers are blending indulgence with functionality. Growth is strong, with predicted gains of +31.7% YoY. Big names like Starbucks, Dunkin, and Chobani are already in the mix, while niche brands like Clean Simple Eats and Jordan’s Skinny Mixes are carving out loyal followings. For moms, SAHMs, and fitness communities, protein coffee is more than a drink — it’s a lifestyle upgrade. Probiotic Soda: Gut Health Goes Mainstream Say goodbye to boring soda. Probiotic soda is on the rise, fueled by rising awareness of gut health and digestive wellness. Though still smaller compared to energy and protein coffee, its growth is dramatic: +79.13% YoY in popularity with predicted +38.5% gains into 2026. TikTok is driving this category too, with 80.1% of its popularity share. Hashtags like #probiotics, #guthealth, and #momsoftiktok reveal how functional wellness is blending with family-friendly appeal. Leading brands Poppi and Olipop have turned soda into a wellness statement, with Poppi seeing 28.0M average weekly views and strong paid promotion fueling awareness. Electrolyte Drinks: Hydration Meets Lifestyle Electrolyte drinks are expanding beyond sports fields into everyday life. Search queries for Gatorade pods, Pedialyte for adults, and cucumber Gatorade show consumers are rethinking hydration as a wellness ritual. The category has +155.8% YoY growth with another +115.4% predicted increase in the coming year. Interestingly, hashtags like #tea, #guthealth, and #bloating are tied to electrolyte conversations, pointing to innovation in formats beyond classic sports drinks. With moms and families driving much of the engagement, this space is evolving into a household essential. Key Takeaways: What The Data Supports Spate’s analysis of functional beverages shows three big shifts shaping the future: Performance Drinks Evolve: Energy drinks are moving beyond caffeine with ingredients that promise focus, endurance, and wellness. Protein + Coffee = Convenience Powerhouse: Busy consumers want functional boosts built into their daily routines. Expect new flavors, formats, and protein blends. Gut Health Everywhere: From probiotic sodas to electrolyte drinks tied to digestion, consumers want beverages that support wellness goals alongside refreshment. What It Means for Brands For brands, the opportunity is clear: consumers want beverages that feel functional, fun, and future-forward. TikTok remains the ultimate launchpad, with most of the category’s top-performing drinks driven by creators, hashtags, and viral recipes. Innovation will thrive where indulgence meets wellness. Think energy sodas with adaptogens, protein coffee creamers, or electrolyte teas for families. With double-digit growth predicted across multiple subcategories, the functional beverage boom is just getting started. Curious which functional flavors or formats are breaking through next? title: Digital Transformation in Banking: From Legacy Systems to AI-Powered Services
summary: Explore how banks are modernizing from legacy systems to AI-powered services, cloud adoption, fraud prevention, DORA adoption, & digital resilience.
body_text: How cloud adoption, regulatory pressure, fraud controls, and AI are reshaping the financial industry's future in 2025 Introduction: Why Digital Transformation is Critical Now The financial services industry has always embraced innovation, but the scale of change today is unprecedented. Fintech startups, neobanks, and Big Tech firms have pushed the envelope, setting new benchmarks for user experience that traditional banks must now match or exceed. Legacy players can no longer rely solely on branch networks and brand trust, as by 2030, the widespread adoption of digital technologies and AI will make banking universally accessible, forcing traditional institutions to accelerate their transformation efforts. Modern customers now expect: • Personalized financial services tailored to their unique needs and life stages • Frictionless 24/7 banking that rivals the best e-commerce platforms • Instant transactions with real-time account updates and notifications • Seamless omnichannel experiences across mobile, web, and physical touchpoints • Proactive financial insights with AI-driven recommendations and alerts The COVID-19 pandemic served as a catalyst, revealing the fragility of traditional banking models as digital adoption soared by 200-300% in some markets while operational bottlenecks highlighted infrastructure inefficiencies. Remote work demands exposed gaps in cloud capabilities, and economic uncertainty increased focus on operational resilience. Today, digital transformation encompasses much more than convenience—it’s about competitiveness, operational resilience, and survival in a rapidly evolving marketplace where customer loyalty is increasingly tied to digital experience quality. Banks must now compete not just with traditional competitors but with technology companies, fintech startups, and digital-native institutions that have built their operations from the ground up with modern infrastructure and customer-centric design principles. The institutions that succeed will be those that can rapidly adapt to changing customer expectations while maintaining the trust and security that customers expect from their financial partners. Cloud vs On-Premise: The Infrastructure Revolution On-premise systems once symbolized security and control, but they have become costly barriers to innovation. Maintenance alone consumes 60-80% of IT budgets in many banks, leaving minimal resources for digital innovation initiatives. Traditional on-premise systems struggle with scalability constraints during peak transaction periods, high maintenance costs requiring specialized technical teams, and difficulty supporting real-time processing demands that modern customers expect from their banking experience. The Cloud Computing Advantage Operational Benefits: • Elastic scaling to handle transaction volume fluctuations during peak periods • Pay-per-use models reducing capital expenditure and improving cost predictability • Faster innovation cycles with rapid deployment capabilities for new services • Global collaboration through centralized platforms and shared resources • Advanced analytics integration with machine learning APIs and real-time processing Strategic Advantages: • Reduced time-to-market for new products by 40-60% • Enhanced disaster recovery capabilities with automated failover systems • Improved regulatory reporting through automated compliance tools • Better customer experience through consistent uptime and performance • Access to cutting-edge technologies without massive infrastructure investments However, regulators continue to stress caution regarding cloud adoption due to dependency risks on major hyperscalers like AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, data sovereignty requirements in Europe and Asia, systemic risk concerns about concentrated cloud infrastructure, and compliance complexity across multiple jurisdictions. As a result, hybrid and multi-cloud architectures are becoming the preferred approach, allowing banks to keep critical core systems on-premise for maximum control while leveraging cloud flexibility for innovation workloads. This balanced approach enables banks to modernize gradually while maintaining regulatory compliance and operational control over their most sensitive systems. The most successful cloud strategies involve careful workload placement, with transaction processing and core banking systems often remaining on-premise while customer-facing applications, analytics platforms, and development environments move to the cloud for maximum agility and innovation potential. DORA Regulation: Reshaping Operational Resilience As we discussed in a prior article about Dora, financial entities and their ICT service providers are required to comply with DORA since January 17, 2025, making this regulation a current priority for banking institutions worldwide. The Digital Operational Resilience Act represents the most comprehensive ICT risk regulation for financial services, fundamentally reshaping how banks approach technology risk management across all operational areas. DORA’s Five Core Pillars 1. ICT Risk Management • Comprehensive governance frameworks with board-level oversight • Regular risk assessments and mitigation strategies • Integration with overall business strategy and risk appetite • Clear accountability structures for ICT-related decisions 2. ICT-Related Incident Management • Standardized incident classification systems across the organization • Rapid response and recovery procedures with defined timelines • Detailed incident documentation and regulatory reporting requirements • Cross-border incident notification protocols for international operations 3. Digital Operational Resilience Testing • Threat intelligence-based red-team testing at designated financial entities • Regular penetration testing requirements with qualified third parties • Scenario-based resilience testing simulating real-world disruptions • Third-party testing validation and ongoing monitoring capabilities The strategic implications for banks are profound, as technology strategy becomes a board-level priority, risk management expands beyond traditional financial risks, continuous monitoring replaces periodic assessments, and vendor relationships require enhanced due diligence. However, these changes also create significant competitive advantages through reputational benefits from demonstrated resilience, customer confidence through operational reliability, improved regulatory relationships via proactive compliance, and operational efficiency through standardized processes. 4. Third-Party ICT Service Provider Management • Due diligence frameworks for vendor selection and ongoing assessment • Contractual security requirements with clear performance metrics • Continuous monitoring of third-party risks and vulnerabilities • Exit strategies for critical service dependencies and vendor transitions 5. Information Sharing • Cyber threat intelligence collaboration across industry participants • Industry-wide vulnerability disclosure with coordinated response efforts • Regulatory authority cooperation and transparent communication • Cross-sector threat information exchange for systemic risk management Banks that embrace DORA proactively will find themselves better positioned to handle not just regulatory requirements but also the increasing sophistication of cyber threats and operational challenges in the digital banking environment. The regulation effectively transforms operational resilience from a compliance requirement into a competitive differentiator for institutions that excel in implementation. Advanced Fraud Prevention in Digital Banking Digital-first banking has exponentially increased fraud opportunities, with criminals now deploying AI-driven attacks, deepfakes, and sophisticated social engineering tactics. In 2025, artificial intelligence has become the most widely adopted banking technology in the banking sector, particularly for fraud detection. The evolution from traditional fraud methods to modern digital techniques has been dramatic and requires equally sophisticated defensive measures. The Evolution of Fraud Tactics Traditional Methods: • Credit card skimming and physical card cloning • Check fraud and document forgery • Phone-based social engineering and identity theft • Account takeover through stolen credentials Modern Digital Techniques: • AI-powered deepfakes for identity impersonation in video calls • Sophisticated phishing campaigns using behavioral analysis and personalization • Account takeover through credential stuffing and automated attacks • Synthetic identity fraud combining real and fabricated information • Business email compromise targeting corporate accounts and wire transfers • Mobile banking malware and SIM swapping attacks on two-factor authentication Banks are responding with sophisticated multi-layered defense strategies that leverage real-time AI analysis across millions of data points for transaction pattern recognition, behavioral biometrics analyzing typing patterns and device usage, geolocation intelligence detecting impossible travel scenarios, and network analysis identifying suspicious device connections. The most advanced systems can process and analyze thousands of variables in milliseconds, making real-time fraud prevention a reality rather than an aspiration. Multi-Layered Defense Systems Real-Time AI Analysis: • Transaction pattern recognition across millions of historical data points • Behavioral biometrics analyzing typing patterns, mouse movements, and device usage • Geolocation intelligence detecting impossible travel scenarios and location anomalies • Network analysis identifying suspicious device connections and IP addresses Advanced Authentication Methods: • Adaptive authentication adjusting security requirements based on real-time risk scores • Biometric verification incorporating voice, fingerprint, facial, and behavioral recognition • Device fingerprinting for trusted device identification and anomaly detection • Behavioral analytics monitoring user interaction patterns and identifying deviations The challenge lies in balancing security with user experience through frictionless authentication that enables invisible fraud detection during normal transactions while implementing step-up authentication only when risks are elevated. Banks are achieving seamless integration with customer journey mapping and deploying personalized security measures based on individual user behavior patterns. This approach ensures that legitimate customers experience smooth, uninterrupted service while potential fraudsters encounter increasingly sophisticated barriers. Collaborative Defense Networks: • Industry consortium participation for real-time threat intelligence sharing • Cross-border cooperation for international fraud prevention and investigation • Regulatory reporting for systemic threat identification and response coordination • Public-private partnerships enhancing overall financial system security AI as the Strategic Transformation Catalyst There is a growing trend towards increased AI adoption, with a strategic focus on revenue generation and developing more sophisticated digital banking experiences, transforming how banks operate and compete. Core AI applications in banking now encompass comprehensive customer experience enhancement and operational efficiency improvements that create measurable business value while improving customer satisfaction and operational resilience. Customer Experience Revolution AI-Powered Service Enhancement: • Natural language processing chatbots providing 24/7 multilingual customer support • Personalized financial advice based on spending patterns, life events, and financial goals • Predictive analytics for proactive service recommendations and financial planning • Voice banking through AI-powered virtual assistants with natural conversation capabilities • Robo-advisors for investment portfolio management and automated rebalancing Operational Efficiency Transformation: • AI-powered automation streamlining core banking operations like security authentication and payment routing • Document processing automation for loan applications, KYC procedures, and regulatory compliance • Intelligent process automation for regulatory reporting and back-office operations • Predictive maintenance for IT infrastructure, ATM networks, and branch technology systems Revolutionary credit assessment capabilities have moved beyond traditional FICO scoring to incorporate alternative data integration including utility payments and social behavior, real-time creditworthiness assessment using transaction history, financial inclusion expansion for underbanked populations, and dynamic risk pricing based on evolving customer profiles. Advanced risk modeling now employs machine learning algorithms for default prediction, portfolio risk optimization using AI-driven scenarios, stress testing automation for regulatory compliance, and market volatility prediction for investment strategies. Responsible AI Implementation These capabilities enable banks to make more accurate lending decisions while expanding access to credit for previously underserved populations, creating both business value and positive social impact. However, responsible AI implementation remains crucial, with regulatory compliance requirements demanding explainable AI systems for transparent decision-making, bias detection and mitigation in algorithmic decisions, comprehensive audit trails for AI-driven processes, and human oversight for critical financial decisions. Ethical AI Considerations: • Fair lending practices ensuring equal access to credit across demographic groups • Privacy protection in data collection, usage, and algorithmic decision-making • Algorithmic transparency for customer trust and regulatory compliance • Continuous monitoring for unintended consequences and model drift • Human oversight maintaining accountability for AI-driven financial decisions Banks that successfully implement AI responsibly will gain competitive advantages while building stronger relationships with both customers and regulators, positioning themselves as trustworthy stewards of financial technology innovation. The key is balancing automation with human judgment, ensuring that AI enhances rather than replaces the human elements that remain crucial for customer trust and complex financial decisions. Comprehensive Business Area Transformation Digital transformation reshapes every aspect of banking operations, creating interconnected improvements across all business lines. The payments revolution encompasses instant payment systems with real-time gross settlement for immediate fund transfers, open banking APIs enabling third-party payment initiation, cross-border payment optimization through blockchain technology, and Central Bank Digital Currencies preparation for future monetary systems. Payments Revolution Instant Payment Systems: • Real-time gross settlement for immediate fund transfers 24/7/365 • Open banking APIs enabling secure third-party payment initiation • Cross-border payment optimization through blockchain and distributed ledger technology • Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) integration and preparation for digital currencies Enhanced Payment Security: • Tokenization for secure card-not-present transactions and data protection • Fraud scoring algorithms for real-time transaction approval and risk assessment • Biometric payment authentication for contactless and mobile transactions • Blockchain-based settlement for transparency, immutability, and reduced counterparty risk These advances collectively create faster, more secure, and more transparent payment experiences that meet evolving customer expectations while reducing operational costs. The integration of multiple payment channels and technologies enables banks to offer comprehensive payment solutions that compete effectively with fintech alternatives while maintaining regulatory compliance and operational control. Digital Lending Transformation Digital lending transformation has revolutionized the customer journey through end-to-end digital experiences featuring automated application processing with AI-powered underwriting, digital document verification using OCR and machine learning, e-signature integration for paperless loan agreements, same-day approval processes for qualified applicants, and mobile-first application experiences optimized for smartphones and tablets. End-to-End Digital Lending: • Automated application processing with AI-powered underwriting and risk assessment • Digital document verification using OCR, machine learning, and blockchain validation • E-signature integration for paperless loan agreements and legal compliance • Same-day approval processes for qualified applicants with automated decision-making • Mobile-first experiences optimized for smartphone and tablet applications Alternative Data Integration: • Open banking data for comprehensive financial profiles and cash flow analysis • Utility payment histories for credit assessment and financial behavior patterns • Social media behavior analysis for fraud detection and identity verification • Rental payment tracking for credit building opportunities and alternative credit scoring This transformation has dramatically reduced loan processing times from weeks to hours while improving accuracy and expanding access to credit for previously underserved populations. The combination of traditional credit data with alternative data sources enables more nuanced risk assessment and broader financial inclusion. Regulatory Compliance and Risk Management Regulatory compliance automation has streamlined KYC and AML processes through AI-driven identity verification using biometric data, automated sanctions screening against global watchlists, pattern recognition for suspicious transaction identification, and real-time compliance monitoring with instant alert systems. Advanced risk management now employs dynamic scenario testing for market volatility, stress model automation for regulatory compliance, predictive forecasting for market shift anticipation, and portfolio optimization using machine learning algorithms. Compliance Automation: • AI-driven identity verification using biometric data and document analysis • Automated sanctions screening against global watchlists and regulatory databases • Pattern recognition for suspicious transaction identification and investigation • Real-time compliance monitoring with instant alert systems and workflow automation Advanced Risk Management: • Dynamic scenario testing for market volatility and stress conditions • Predictive forecasting for market shifts and portfolio optimization • Automated stress testing for regulatory compliance and capital planning • Machine learning algorithms for portfolio risk assessment and optimization These comprehensive transformations create synergies across business areas, enabling banks to operate more efficiently while providing superior customer service and maintaining robust compliance postures. The interconnected nature of these improvements means that advances in one area often enhance capabilities in others, creating compound benefits from digital transformation investments. Overcoming Transformation Challenges Digital transformation faces significant organizational and technical barriers that require strategic approaches to overcome. Cultural and organizational barriers represent some of the most persistent challenges, as addressing cultural inertia requires comprehensive change management programs with executive sponsorship, digital literacy training for all staff levels, innovation incentives rewarding digital adoption, and cross-generational collaboration bridging digital divides. Cultural and Organizational Transformation Addressing Cultural Barriers: • Change management programs with dedicated executive sponsorship and clear communication • Digital literacy training for all staff levels, from entry-level to senior management • Innovation incentives rewarding digital adoption and creative problem-solving • Success story communication showcasing transformation benefits and individual contributions • Cross-generational collaboration bridging digital divides and knowledge transfer Leadership and Governance Evolution: • Digital transformation committees with C-level representation and decision-making authority • Clear accountability frameworks for transformation initiatives and measurable outcomes • Regular progress monitoring with key performance indicators and milestone tracking • Resource allocation strategies prioritizing high-impact projects and sustainable funding The competition for digital talent in banking has intensified, requiring institutions to offer compelling value propositions that combine traditional banking stability with cutting-edge technology opportunities. Strategic partnerships with universities for talent pipeline development, continuous learning programs for existing staff upskilling, specialized recruitment strategies for cybersecurity and AI expertise, and external consultant utilization for knowledge transfer have become essential components of successful transformation programs. Technical and Integration Solutions Technical and integration challenges are equally complex, with legacy system integration requiring API-first architectures enabling gradual system replacement, middleware solutions bridging legacy and modern systems, data migration strategies ensuring continuity during transitions, and parallel processing capabilities maintaining service availability throughout modernization efforts. Legacy System Integration: • API-first architectures enabling gradual system replacement and modernization • Middleware solutions bridging legacy and modern systems with minimal disruption • Data migration strategies ensuring continuity and integrity during system transitions • Parallel processing capabilities maintaining service availability during upgrades Cybersecurity and Risk Management: • Zero-trust security architectures assuming no implicit trust and verifying all access • Continuous security monitoring with AI-powered threat detection and response • Incident response planning with regular simulation exercises and team training • Third-party security assessments for comprehensive vendor risk management Cybersecurity and risk management challenges have expanded dramatically as digital transformation increases the attack surface for potential threats. The interconnected nature of modern banking systems means that a security breach in one area can potentially impact multiple business lines, making comprehensive security planning essential. Successful transformation requires viewing these challenges not as obstacles but as opportunities to build more resilient, efficient, and customer-focused operations that can adapt to future changes in technology and market conditions. Strategic Roadmap for Digital Banking Success Digital transformation requires a comprehensive, strategic approach that balances innovation with risk management and regulatory compliance. The essential implementation framework provides a structured pathway for banks to achieve sustainable digital transformation while managing risks and maintaining operational excellence throughout the process. Phase-Based Implementation Strategy Phase 1: Foundation Building (Months 1-6) • Current state assessment of existing technology, processes, and organizational readiness • Digital strategy development aligned with business objectives and market positioning • Governance framework establishment including risk management and compliance structures • Initial pilot project selection for quick wins, learning opportunities, and stakeholder buy-in Phase 2: Core System Modernization (Months 6-18) • Cloud migration strategy implementation with hybrid approach and risk mitigation • API development for system integration and third-party connectivity enablement • Data architecture modernization enabling real-time analytics and decision-making • Security framework enhancement meeting DORA requirements and industry best practices This foundation phase is critical for establishing the organizational readiness and strategic direction necessary for successful transformation. The modernization phase focuses on building the technical infrastructure and capabilities that will support advanced digital services and customer experiences. Phase 3: AI and Advanced Analytics (Months 12-24) • Machine learning model development for fraud detection, customer insights, and operational optimization • Automated decision-making systems for lending, risk assessment, and customer service • Predictive analytics implementation for business optimization and strategic planning • Customer experience personalization through AI-driven recommendations and services Phase 4: Ecosystem Integration (Months 18-36) • Open banking API deployment for third-party integration and partnership enablement • Strategic partnership development with fintechs, technology providers, and ecosystem players • Advanced compliance automation for regulatory efficiency and risk management • Innovation lab establishment for continuous experimentation and future technology adoption Success Metrics and Performance Indicators Operational Excellence Metrics: • System uptime improvement targeting 99.9% availability with minimal planned downtime • Transaction processing speed enhancement by 50-80% across all customer touchpoints • Cost reduction of 15-25% through automation and operational efficiency improvements • Regulatory compliance efficiency measured by audit findings, regulatory feedback, and compliance costs Customer Experience Indicators: • Digital adoption rates across all customer segments and demographic groups • Net Promoter Score (NPS) improvement in digital channels and overall customer satisfaction • Customer acquisition cost reduction through digital marketing and automated onboarding • Service resolution time decrease by 60-70% through AI-powered support and self-service options Business Growth Measurements: • Revenue from digital channels increasing by 30-50% year-over-year • New product time-to-market reduction by 40-60% through agile development processes • Market share growth in digital banking segments and competitive positioning • Cross-selling success rates improvement through AI recommendations and personalized offerings Future-Proofing and Emerging Technologies Future-proofing strategies prepare banks for emerging technologies including quantum computing readiness for encryption and optimization challenges, blockchain integration for transparent and secure transactions, Internet of Things connectivity for contextual banking and smart device integration, and augmented reality applications for enhanced customer experience and remote service delivery. Emerging Technology Preparation: • Quantum computing readiness for future encryption challenges and computational optimization • Blockchain integration for transparent transactions and smart contract automation • IoT connectivity for contextual banking and smart device ecosystem integration • Augmented reality applications for enhanced customer experience and remote advisory services Regulatory Adaptation Framework: • Continuous compliance monitoring for evolving regulations and international standards • Global regulatory harmonization preparation for cross-border operations • ESG integration in digital services and sustainable banking practices • Privacy-first architecture anticipating data protection evolution and customer expectations Banks that successfully implement this comprehensive roadmap will be well-positioned to thrive in an increasingly digital and competitive financial services landscape. The key to success lies in maintaining flexibility while building robust foundations, enabling continuous adaptation to changing customer needs, regulatory requirements, and technological capabilities. Conclusions Digital transformation represents a fundamental shift in how banks operate, compete, and serve customers. Success requires balancing technological innovation with operational resilience, regulatory compliance, and customer trust. The banking institutions that will thrive in the digital age are those that embrace comprehensive change while maintaining the fundamental values of trust, security, and customer service that define successful financial institutions. Thriving Digital Banks Will: • Implement robust IT governance frameworks meeting DORA requirements and industry best practices • Adopt flexible hybrid cloud strategies optimizing performance, compliance, and innovation capabilities • Deploy responsible AI with transparency, ethical considerations, and continuous monitoring • Invest significantly in fraud prevention, cybersecurity resilience, and operational security • Cultivate digital-first cultures throughout their organizations while preserving customer-centric values These successful institutions will focus on sustainable growth by prioritizing customer experience in all digital initiatives, building scalable architectures supporting future innovation and market expansion, developing strategic partnerships with fintech and technology providers, maintaining operational excellence while pursuing digital innovation, and creating sustainable competitive advantages through data analytics and AI capabilities. The transformation extends beyond technology implementation to encompass fundamental changes in organizational culture, customer relationships, and business models that position banks as true digital service providers rather than traditional financial intermediaries. Banks achieving this comprehensive transformation will not only reduce operational costs but also unlock new revenue streams, strengthen customer relationships, and build resilient operations capable of thriving in an increasingly digital financial services ecosystem. The Future Success Framework: • Seamless technology integration with human-centered design and customer experience focus • Proactive regulatory compliance turning requirements into competitive advantages • Continuous innovation culture balanced with operational stability and risk management • Ecosystem partnerships enabling comprehensive financial service offerings • Sustainable growth models based on data-driven insights and AI-powered capabilities The future belongs to institutions that seamlessly merge cutting-edge technology, regulatory compliance, and human-centered design into their core operating models, creating banking experiences that are simultaneously more efficient, secure, and personally relevant than ever before. This transformation is not optional—it is essential for survival and success in the rapidly evolving financial services landscape of 2025 and beyond. title: Federated GraphQL Schema Testing in CI/CD with WunderGraph and Sandboxes
summary: Prevent breaking changes in your federated GraphQL API. Learn how to combine WunderGraph with branch-based sandboxes for automated schema validation in your CI/CD pipeline.
body_text: Introduction One of the common challenges when working with GraphQL is managing schema evolution , especially testing changes introduced in a subgraph of a federated API (e.g in a git branch) without disrupting the GraphQL API deployed in a shared environment like staging. This document presents an approach to address that challenge by combining WunderGraph with Signadot Sandboxes , enabling you to validate schema updates in an isolated environment while preserving baseline reliability. Baseline Environment Before we explore how to integrate Sandboxes with WunderGraph, let’s define the baseline environment . We’ll follow the setup described in the WunderGraph Cosmo Cloud Onboarding guide, but adapt it to run on Kubernetes (using a local minikube cluster for this demo). Prerequisites: kubectl and minikube installed A WunderGraph Cosmo account The wgc CLI installed and authenticated A Signadot account and the operator installed in the cluster The signadot CLI installed and authenticated Steps Run the following commands to prepare your environment: Validation At this point, your federated graph should be active and visible in the WunderGraph Cosmo Console . You can open the console to verify that all subgraphs have been registered and the router is healthy. You can also explore the router’s GraphQL playground locally using Signadot: 1. Start the local connection: 2. Open the router playground in your browser: http://router.wundergraph-demo.svc:3002/ 3. Paste the following GraphQL query into the editor: Using Sandboxes To achieve our goal of introducing schema changes without impacting the baseline environment, we’ll leverage WunderGraph’s Feature Flags capability. Here’s how it all fits together: 1. Create a fork of the products service using the products_fg image (an alternative version of the products service where some schema updates were introduced). 2. Using the resulting sandbox routing key from above (referred to as ), create a WunderGraph feature subgraph and a corresponding feature flag: You can generalize the procedure above for multiple services as follows: These two steps can easily be automated in a CI pipeline : first detect the services that have changed, then create the sandbox, and finally configure and register the feature flag once everything is ready. Validation If you open the router playground again, this time under the context of the sandbox you created (in this demo we are using the browser extension to do so), you’ll notice a new property available on the employee type: the productCount field, which is served by the products_fg fork. If you run the same query against the baseline environment , you’ll receive an error because the productCount field isn’t implemented there. How it Works WunderGraph’s feature flags operate via the X-Feature-Flag header . Because the Signadot routing key is typically propagated through standard context propagation mechanisms, such as W3C Trace Context and Baggage , we needed a way to convert it into the appropriate feature-flag header. To achieve this, we added a proxy in front of the WunderGraph Router within the deployment. This proxy intercepts requests, extracts the routing key, translates it into the X-Feature-Flag header, and then forwards the request to the actual Router. For example, if an incoming request includes the following header: After passing through the proxy, the request will look like this: The proxy simply extracts the sd-routing-key value from the Baggage header and adds it as an X-Feature-Flag header, leaving the original Baggage header untouched. Therefore, the request flow works as shown in the diagram below: 1. A client request arrives at the Envoy proxy (inside the Router Pod) on port 3002 . 2. The proxy translates the sd-routing-key (found in the Baggage header) into the X-Feature-Flag header, then forwards the request to the WunderGraph Router (port 13002 ). 3. The WunderGraph Router loads the updated schema (enabled by the feature flag). 4. To resolve the query, it sends a request to the configured routing endpoint, which points to the original service URL. 5. Because the request includes the Signadot routing key , the DevMesh Proxy forwards it to the forked service ( Products FG ), where the experimental schema changes are available. Alternatives In an ideal scenario, we could eliminate the translation proxy in front of the Router.Since Signadot supports sandbox routing using custom headers , if the underlying system were able to propagate the X-Feature-Flag header directly, we could configure it as a custom routing header in the Signadot Operator. In that case, all routing logic could run entirely off X-Feature-Flag , removing the need for an extra proxy layer. Another option is to extend or fork the WunderGraph Router (which is open source) to add support for custom headers. This would allow the Router to read the feature flag directly from the Baggage header, avoiding the translation step altogether. Conclusion By combining WunderGraph feature flags with Signadot Sandboxes , you can introduce and validate schema changes in a safe, isolated environment without disrupting basline traffic. This approach provides a clean workflow for experimenting with new fields or subgraphs, testing them end-to-end, and rolling them out with confidence. While the current setup relies on a lightweight proxy to translate routing keys into feature-flag headers, future improvements could simplify the architecture even further. Adopting this pattern helps teams move faster while maintaining reliability, making it a practical strategy for evolving federated GraphQL schemas in modern Kubernetes environments.
